title: Local State vs Server State
description: Understand the fundamental difference between local UI state and server state, and learn when to use each pattern in your Next.js applications.

data.text: Every interactive web application manages two very different kinds of state. **Local state** lives in the browser and controls how your interface looks and behaves in the moment. **Server state** lives on your database or API, and represents the actual data your app fetches from the outside world. Understanding the distinction is one of the most important foundations of building reliable React and Next.js applications.

For years, developers stored everything in a single global store. But modern React and Next.js encourage us to treat these two kinds of state differently — because they have different lifecycles, different rules, and different tools designed specifically for them.

Local state is any state that belongs to a single component or a small part of your UI. It is created with `useState` or `useReducer`, lives only in the browser, and disappears when the user closes the tab. Examples include: whether a dropdown menu is open, the current value of a search input, which tab is active, or whether a modal is visible.

data.title: Local State with useState
Rule of Thumb
data.text: If the state would not matter if the user refreshed the page, it is almost certainly local state. The open/closed state of a menu is local. A user's profile data is not.

Server state is data that originates from a server — a database, a REST API, or GraphQL endpoint. It is the source of truth outside your application. Your React components consume it, display it, and sometimes modify it, but they do not own it.

items: A list of blog posts fetched from your CMS
A user's profile loaded from your database
Search results returned by an API
Product inventory from an e-commerce backend

data.text: Server state comes with concerns that local state does not have: caching, background refetching, loading and error states, deduplication of requests, and invalidation when data changes. These concerns are so common that dedicated libraries like TanStack Query (React Query) were built to handle them.

rows: Fetch libraries or framework data hooks
Via query cache or global store
Modal open, input value, active tab

data.text: When you treat server state like local state, you end up writing a lot of custom code to solve problems that existing tools already handle. You might store API responses in `useState`, manually track loading flags, and write complex `useEffect` logic to refetch data. This approach is fragile and scales poorly.
By separating the two, you can pick the right tool for each job: `useState` for ephemeral UI concerns, and React Query or Next.js Server Components for data that belongs to the server.

data.title: Server State with React Query
Common Mistake
data.text: Do not put server data in useState unless you have a very specific reason. React Query, SWR, or Next.js data fetching patterns handle caching, deduplication, and background updates automatically. Reimplementing these features yourself is a common source of bugs.

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Local state controls UI behavior; server state represents remote data
Use useState for ephemeral UI concerns like toggles and inputs
Use React Query, SWR, or Next.js data patterns for server state
Separating the two lets you use specialized tools for each problem
